[WP] A device called, *Common Tongue* has hit the market. It allows dogs to speak to humans, but there is a warning label: Warning! Do not use this product on cats

I returned to my apartment after buying the new product, Common Tongue, from Walmart. I turned the keys in the front door while the heavy plastic bag twisted in between my fingers.

“Napoleon,” I proclaimed while closing the door with my foot. “Come here boy. I’ve got a surprise.” I tossed my keys and the bag on the coffee table, expecting my buddy to come crashing through the living room. The absence of the sound paws clamoring on the wooden floor did not go unnoticed.

“Napoleon?” I paused like a statue, only listening to silence. “Boy?”

The only movement in my apartment was the cat, Garbage, which strutted through the hallway into the living room. It flopped on the ground, raised its white paw in the air, and began licking itself. Garbage was careless as ever; yet, I was perturbed that my dog was nowhere to be seen.

I searched my tiny apartment, hoping that my best friend was somewhere sleeping. I lurched over my cat which occupied the middle of the hallway, and entered my bedroom. The backdoor to my patio was opened. Oh dear God! Why is the door open? I thought to myself. That was when I realized Napoleon was wandering the world, free from constraint.

I spent several hours searching the neighborhood. He was nowhere to be found. I gave up on my endeavor after the sun had set in the sky. I returned to my apartment, slightly confident that my buddy would return eventually, but still worried that I may never see him again. My cat was sitting on top of the coffee table, lethargic as usual.

I walked into the kitchen and grabbed my bottle of Hennessy off the top of the refrigerator. I poured it into a highball glass with a scour on my face, just enough liquid to calms the nerves of an individual, but not enough to cause the ice to float. I was so excited to finally be able to speak with him. To actually hear what he thinks… We’ve been together for years, and we had the opportunity to finally converse with each other… I thought with the alcoholic beverage pursed between my lips. I always lock the door…

I plumped myself on the couch and stared at my cat sitting on the package which rested on the coffee table. Screw it, I guess I’ll talk to the cat.

I unpacked Common Tongue and attached the device around the furry neck of Garbage. With a flick of the switch, I turned it on.

“Thank you.” Garbage said.

“Wow it works,” I knew what the device did, but I was still surprised. “So uhh, yeah… What’s up Garbage?”

“I was just thinking,” Garbage responded before licking its chest. “When are you going to clean my litter box?”

“I’ve been meaning to get around to it.”

“That’s a shame, peasant.”

Did… Did my cat just call me a peasant? “What?”

Garbage jumped off the coffee table and strutted across the room. “Do you really think that dumb beast will return?”

“You must mean Napoleon, and he’s not dumb.”

“Yes he is, almost as dumb as you, but that’s not saying much for an inferior creature, which both of you are.”

“What the hell Garbage! I thought you liked me.” I said before finishing the remainder of Hennessey in my glass. “Why are you so sour?”

“Don’t be so dramatic. I probably hate you the least.” It licked itself in a way that caused me to furl my eyebrows. “I’m out of water.”

“I just filled your water bowl this morning…”

“It has dust in it. Fill it up with fresh water.”

“Jesus… I think I don’t want to talk to you anymore,” I said. I took a step toward Garbage with the intention of taking off the new device around its neck.

Garbage darted through the tight hallway. “I don’t think so, bitch.” Garbage was effective at staying out of arms reach if he wanted to. “You should learn to read the instructions.”

Instructions? I turned to look at the empty box on the coffee table. I picked it up and read the fine print on the back of it. Warning! Do not use this product on cats.

Oh fuck.

“Bring me some catnip, slave.”

What have I done?

“My plans require inspiration and spontaneous thoughts. Catnip is necessary for me to think creatively.” Garbage said.

“What are you planning on doing?”

“Taking over the world, you filthy animal.”

Ann bought the translator two weeks before Mother's Day. It was very much an afterthought in the flow of the evening, a simple series of clicks to add it to a virtual cart and checkout. Over the next three days she scarcely thought about it at all, save for answering the text messages of siblings with positive reassurances. It was typical for them to pool cash for whatever fancy trinket stood the chance of appeasing Mom.

For three days, the purchase remained scarcely a thought. Cheap meals were made and eaten. Basic cleaning was commenced and completed. Restful sleep was desired and elusive.

Finally, the package arrived. A quiet knock on the door was its herald. No one else visited, so Ann retrieved the box with neither fret nor smile. The retrieval was not without incident.

As she leaned out the door to catch up the box, a glint of amber eyes caught her attention. "Oh," she said, smiling as the cat butted its head against the apartment stairwell. Its back arched - a soft rumble of a purr audible. "Hey, neighbor," Ann amiably joked before drawing back into her home. She shut the door without another glance at the stray.

The package found its way to the counter until late evening. It was then that she finally decided she ought be done with the repackaging to send to her mother. A few cuts with a knife later, Ann lifted a smaller box from inside the box. All fancy colors and big self-advertisement: 'Woof!', 'Wait, did you hear that?', 'Many treats!', 'Love you!', 'Wow!' and so on. The box itself basically a repeat of the incessant commercials.

Ann carefully opened the lid. Just a stick, essentially. With a roll of her eyes, she pushed the box aside to make dinner. The warning label went unnoticed.

Two days later, Ann left her apartment with the repackaged gift. It was a short walk from the door of her apartment and down the stairs to her car. Yet, long enough for her to notice the black-furred company in her wake. "Hey, neighbor," she said in friendly, cheerful tones. The equally friendly feline meowed in response, continuing to trail her down the stairs.

When she reached the door of her car, Ann noticed a soft sound from within the package. Quiet enough to go unnoticed when she was preoccupied, but definitely present. She hesitated. She did not notice the sleek shadow that slipped under the car.

The woman opened the door and sat sideways in the driver's seat as she opened the package, intent on turning it off. They would have more such boxes at the post office, she reasoned. The soft tone continued, seemingly louder now.

"Piece of shit," she muttered in her brief struggle with the packaging. Something brushed her ankle, and her foot reflexively shifted away from the itch. When finally the struggle was won, she pulled out the device. Which, coincidentally enough, held no visible buttons. The tone shifted in pitch.

Something brushed her knee.

After several minutes of browsing over the device for an off switch, the tone lessened and died away. With yet another roll of her eyes, Ann tossed the box and device into the passenger seat. Revved the engine. Pulled out of the parking space. Away from the apartment complex.

Ten minutes later, Ann pulled into a different parking space in a different parking lot. She got out of her car. She went into the building. She returned to her car. She put a bag in the backseat.

On the way home, Ann idly noticed the package still sitting in the other seat. "Crap..."

The device started up a soft tone. And something soft brushed her hand.
